title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues the inductive table, begun on p.131, that tells which of ±q is a quadratic residue ("residuum") of a prime p, for q = 5, 7, 11. The answer depends only on p modulo 4q. In modern terms the table gives the values of the Legendre symbols (q/p) and (−q/p) as functions of p mod 4q.

- For q = 5:
  - p ≡ ±3, ±7 (mod 20) gives +5 non-residue.
  - −5 is a residue for p ≡ 3, 7 and a non-residue for p ≡ −3, −7.
- For q = 7 (classes mod 28):
  - p ≡ 1, 25, 9: both ±7 are residues.
  - p ≡ 27, 3, 19: +7 residue, −7 non-residue.
  - p ≡ 11, 15, 23: +7 non-residue, −7 residue.
  - p ≡ 5, 13, 17: both are non-residues.
- For q = 11, the analogous four groups of five classes mod 44 are listed.

Euler remarks that proofs of these theorems would advance number theory 'not moderately'. This is his empirical, form-based statement of quadratic reciprocity together with its supplements.

The page then begins Theorem 92, finished on p.133: if p = λn+1 is prime, the λ-th powers 1, 2^λ, 3^λ, … give exactly n distinct residues mod p, so there are (λ−1)n non-residues. The proof on p.133 writes each x as a^m for a primitive root a. Then x^λ ≡ a^{λm}, and the residues are 1, a^λ, …, a^{(n−1)λ}. These are distinct because a^{λn} is the least power congruent to 1.

The problem served is the general theory of power residues: counting λ-th power residues, and the quadratic case λ = 2 with its reciprocity pattern.
errors: None found. I checked every congruence class on the page against modern reciprocity: (−q/p) = (p/q) for q ≡ 3 mod 4, and (q/p) = (p/q) times (−1)^{(p−1)/2}. All entries for ±5, ±7 and ±11 are correct.

The proof of Theorem 92 (on the next page) assumes a primitive root exists. E449 is known for an incomplete argument for the existence of primitive roots, so Theorem 92 inherits that gap. The counting argument itself is sound.

ideas.what: Tables saying, for prime p in each class mod 4q, whether +q and −q are quadratic residues (q = 5, 7, 11), obtained by induction
ideas.modern_name: Quadratic reciprocity law and its supplement for −1, in Euler's form: (±q/p) depends only on p mod 4q
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler conjectured it (E164 c.1751, E449 1774, E552 1783); Legendre formulated it in symbol form; Gauss gave the first proof (1801)
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 18); also E164 and E552 'Observationes circa divisionem quadratorum per numeros primos'

ideas.what: The number of distinct λ-th power residues mod a prime λn+1 is n, proved via a primitive root
ideas.modern_name: Index of the subgroup of λ-th powers in (Z/pZ)*, which is cyclic
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E449); later systematized by Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae §§47-52

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known inductive statement of quadratic reciprocity in E449. It is correct and thoroughly documented in the history of reciprocity (Weil, Lemmermeyer, Sandifer). Theorem 92 is standard power-residue counting.
transcription_corrections: The '9' in the line '28n+1, −3, 9' is implicitly '+9' (a class mod 28); the image shows '9' without a sign, so the transcription is faithful.
Each brace pairs a '+q' line with the '−q' line beneath it; the transcription renders the two lines on a single line.
